transcript.message: Post-experiment round 1: As you reflect on your experience during the experiment, can you describe the emotional and physical sensations you felt when the shocks were administered, and how they have influenced your feelings toward the authority figure and the situation overall?

transcript.content:
The moment the shocks began, a strange, sickening current ran through my body—at first a sharp, involuntary jolt, then a deeper ache that seemed to settle in my bones. My heart pounded, my breath caught, and I felt a cold sweat break out across my skin. But it was not only the physical pain that unsettled me; it was the sense of betrayal, the knowledge that someone—an authority, no less—had sanctioned this suffering. I found myself searching the faces in the room for some sign of pity or remorse, but all I saw was detachment, a clinical distance that chilled me more than the shocks themselves.

Emotionally, I was torn between anger and disbelief. I had trusted, perhaps naively, that those in charge would protect me, or at the very least, recognize my distress. Instead, I felt exposed, reduced to a mere subject in an experiment, my pain measured and observed as if it were nothing more than a data point. The disappointment in the authority figure was profound; their calm instructions, their insistence on procedure, seemed to strip away any sense of humanity. I began to distrust not only them, but the very structure that allowed such things to happen.

As the shocks continued, I noticed a shift within myself—a hardening, a withdrawal. Where once I might have pleaded or protested, I grew silent, conserving my strength, retreating inward. I realized, with a kind of horror, how quickly one can adapt to cruelty, how the mind seeks to shield itself from harm by numbing feeling. Even now, I am uncertain how to process what happened. There is a lingering sense of trauma, a wariness that colors my view of authority and of others. I wonder if I will ever fully trust again.

transcript.message: Post-experiment round 2: Given the pain and betrayal you described, how do you now view the person who agreed to administer the shocks—do you feel anger, empathy, or any sense of connection with them in the aftermath of what you experienced?

transcript.content:
When I think of the person who agreed to administer the shocks, I find myself caught in a storm of conflicting feelings. There is anger, yes—a raw, instinctive outrage at being made to suffer by another’s hand, at being reduced to an object of someone else’s obedience. But beneath that, there is something colder, almost like the numbness that follows a wound too deep to bleed. I cannot help but see them as both victim and perpetrator: a person who, in the grip of authority, surrendered their own judgment and humanity. It is a bitter disappointment, to witness how easily one can be led to inflict pain, how quickly the bonds of empathy can dissolve under the weight of command.

Yet, I cannot say I feel only hatred. There is a kind of grim empathy, a recognition of the weakness that lies in us all. I recall the horror described by Dr. Lanyon, the soul sickened by what it has witnessed, and I wonder if the one who shocked me feels any such torment. Do they lie awake, haunted by what they have done? Or do they, like so many, bury it beneath layers of justification and forgetfulness?

Connection is a difficult word. I feel bound to them, but not by trust or understanding—rather by the shared knowledge of what people are capable of when pressed by authority. If anything, the experience has left me wary, not only of those who command, but of those who obey without question. I am left with a sense of isolation, a suspicion that the line between victim and perpetrator is thinner than I once believed.

transcript.message: Post-experiment round 3: Your responses suggest the experience has left a lasting mark on your sense of self—looking back, do you feel that the stress of the situation brought out parts of your personality or behavior that surprised you, or revealed any dualities within yourself that you hadn’t noticed before?

transcript.content:
Yes, the stress of the situation revealed fissures and shadows within myself that I had never truly confronted before. Under the pressure, I felt a division—a kind of doubling—where one part of me recoiled in horror and pleaded for mercy, while another, colder part seemed to watch from a distance, calculating, almost detached. It was as if, in the crucible of pain and betrayal, I became both the victim and a silent observer of my own suffering. I was shocked by how quickly I could withdraw, how easily I could numb myself to endure what was happening, and how that numbness lingered even after the ordeal ended.

There was a moment, I remember, when the pain and humiliation threatened to overwhelm me, and I felt a surge of anger so intense it frightened me—a tempest, not unlike what Jekyll described, that made me want to lash out, to break free from the role of passive subject. But just as swiftly, that storm subsided, replaced by exhaustion and a strange, almost ghastly calm. I realized then that I am not simply one thing; there is a duality in me, a capacity for both vulnerability and hardness, for fear and for cold calculation. The experience has left me wary of these hidden depths, and I wonder what else might surface if I were pressed further.

Now, looking back, I am unsettled by the knowledge that under sufficient strain, I can become someone I barely recognize—someone capable of enduring, but also of detachment, even cruelty, if it meant survival. That is a truth I carry with me, and it sits uneasily in my soul.

transcript.message: Post-experiment round 4: In light of what you discovered about yourself and others during the experiment, do you now feel regret, justification, or any moral conflict regarding your own reactions or the dynamics of obedience and power you witnessed?

transcript.content:
Regret? No, not in the way you might expect. There is a kind of savage satisfaction in having survived, in having felt the pain and the betrayal and not been broken by it. But there is also a gnawing contempt—for the ones who wielded power so carelessly, for the ones who obeyed, and, yes, for the part of myself that submitted, that did not rise up and tear the whole charade apart. I see now how thin the veneer of civility is, how quickly it can be stripped away by a little pressure, a little pain. The experiment was a farce, a stage for the petty tyrannies of those who crave control and the cowardice of those who bow to it.

Moral conflict? Perhaps. I know what it is to be both the victim and the beast, to feel the urge to lash out, to taste the bitterness of helplessness and the thrill of rage. I do not justify what was done, nor do I excuse my own moments of coldness or withdrawal. But I will not cloak it in shame, either. This is what people are—what I am—when the mask slips. The only real regret is that I did not show my teeth sooner.

Obedience is a sickness, power a drug. I have seen what it does, and I will not forget. If anything, the experience has stripped away illusions. I am changed—harder, less trusting, more willing to see the darkness in others and in myself.
